pool.prompt: A splicer needs to open a loose-tube OSP cable. What is the correct tool/method for slitting the outer jacket without damaging the buffer tubes inside?
choices: A sharp knife — score along the length with light pressure
The ripcord (or a purpose-built ring-type cable slitting tool) — pulled lengthwise, it slits the jacket cleanly without risking the buffer tubes below
A hacksaw — the steel armor below the jacket protects the buffer tubes
Diagonal cutters — snip the end of the jacket and peel it back
pool.explanation: The ripcord is built into the cable for exactly this purpose — grab it and pull lengthwise to slit the jacket cleanly. A knife risks cutting into the buffer tubes and damaging fibers; diagonal cutters can crush buffer tubes.
pool.citation: ICEA S-87-640, Standard for Optical Fiber Outside Plant Communications Cable (loose-tube OSP cable construction).

pool.prompt: What is the purpose of water-blocking gel inside a buffer tube?
choices: To lubricate the fibers during fusion splicing
To prevent water from migrating along the cable length if the jacket is breached
To act as an electrical insulator between fibers
To cushion the fibers against impact damage
pool.explanation: Water-blocking gel is a petroleum-based compound filling the buffer tube. If the jacket and armor are damaged — say, from a dig-in — the gel physically blocks water from migrating along the cable via the buffer tube to a splice case, which could otherwise flood a splice location miles away by capillary action.
pool.citation: ICEA S-87-640 (OSP cable construction — water-blocking requirements).

pool.prompt: In a figure-8 aerial cable installation, what is the name of the component that carries all the mechanical tension between poles, so the fiber cable itself carries none?
choices: Central member
Messenger
Ripcord
Armor
pool.explanation: The steel messenger wire is lashed alongside the fiber cable in a figure-8 configuration. At each pole, the messenger — not the fiber cable — is clamped and takes all the aerial tension load. This protects the fibers from the bending and stretching that direct tension would cause.
pool.citation: ICEA S-87-640 Annex D (figure-8 aerial self-supporting cable construction).

pool.prompt: A job spec requires "dielectric cable" for an aerial installation. Which is a valid reason this requirement might be specified?
choices: Dielectric cable has lower attenuation than metallic-armored cable
Dielectric cable contains no metal, so it needs no bonding/grounding at each pole — useful where no ground continuity on the cable is wanted, or near high-voltage lines
Dielectric cable is always cheaper than armored cable for aerial use
Dielectric cable is required by RUS for all aerial fiber installations
pool.explanation: Dielectric (all-glass/all-plastic, no-metal) cable requires no bonding or grounding, which matters where a non-metallic cable is preferred — for example, near high-voltage lines or where no ground-continuity path on the cable itself is wanted. ADSS (All-Dielectric Self-Supporting) is the common aerial dielectric option.
pool.citation: ICEA S-87-640 Annex F (all-dielectric self-supporting cable).

pool.prompt: What does ICEA S-87-640 formally cover, and what do its Annex D and Annex F sections address?
choices: Indoor patch cable connectors; Annex D covers SC connectors, Annex F covers LC connectors
The Standard for Optical Fiber Outside Plant Communications Cable; Annex D covers figure-8 aerial self-supporting cable, Annex F covers all-dielectric self-supporting (ADSS) cable
FCC pole attachment rate rules; Annex D and F have no cable-construction content
NESC clearance rules for aerial fiber; Annex D/F are reserved for future revisions
pool.explanation: ICEA S-87-640 is the industry standard for OSP fiber cable intended for outdoor use — aerial, direct-buried, or in duct. Annex D adds requirements specific to figure-8 aerial self-supporting cable; Annex F covers all-dielectric self-supporting (ADSS) cable.
pool.citation: ICEA S-87-640, formal scope and annex structure.

pool.prompt: How can a splicer tell whether an OSP cable jacket is LSZH (Low-Smoke Zero-Halogen) rated, given that OSP jackets are standardly black regardless of type?
choices: By the jacket color — LSZH cable always ships in a distinct color
By reading the printed legend on the jacket (looking for "LSZH," "OFNR," or "OFNP" in the print) — TIA-598 does not use jacket color to distinguish OSP cable types or ratings
By the diameter of the cable — LSZH cable is always thinner
There is no way to identify LSZH cable without lab testing
pool.explanation: Standard OSP cable jackets are black HDPE, and the carbon black itself provides UV resistance — colored pigments can't match it, so TIA-598 does not use jacket color as an OSP type/rating indicator. LSZH (and indoor ratings like OFNR/OFNP) are identified by the printed legend on the jacket, not by color. A non-black jacket on OSP cable is a vendor-specific variant, not a standard color convention.
pool.citation: TIA-598 (fiber cable color coding standard — scope does not extend jacket color to type/rating identification).

pool.prompt: Inside a buffer tube, individual fibers are identified using a repeating color sequence. How many distinct colors make up that base sequence before it repeats (with a stripe marker) on higher fiber counts?
choices: 6 colors
8 colors
12 colors
24 colors
pool.explanation: TIA-598 defines a 12-color sequence used for both individual fiber coloring and buffer tube coloring. For fiber/tube counts beyond 12, the same 12-color sequence repeats with an added stripe or binder marker to distinguish the repeat group (e.g., fibers 13-24 repeat the 12 colors with a contrasting stripe).

pool.prompt: Match each layer of a standard loose-tube OSP cable to its primary function.

items.label: UV/moisture barrier against the outside world
Lets you slit the jacket open without damaging what's inside
Holds a group of fibers in water-blocking gel
Gives the cable its shape; anchored in the splice case

pool.explanation: From outside in: the HDPE jacket resists UV and moisture; the ripcord lets you open the jacket cleanly; buffer tubes hold groups of fibers in water-blocking gel; the central member (steel or GRP rod) gives the cable its shape and must be anchored inside the splice case so cable tension doesn't pull through and break the splices.
pool.citation: ICEA S-87-640 (standard loose-tube OSP cable layer construction).
